title: Digital Innovation & Big Data/AI — Chapter 3
subtitle: EPITA D&I4DBT Course, pages 5–63: Digital Transformation, AI fundamentals, Big Data, GenAI, value chains, adoption barriers, triple challenge, combinatorial effects.

questions.question: According to Thesis #1 in the course, digital transformation is primarily the consequence of:
options: Government regulation mandating technology upgrades
Technology adoption by individuals and organizations
Invention of new hardware components in research labs
Decline of traditional manufacturing industries
questions.explanation: Thesis #1 states explicitly: 'Digital Transformation is the consequence of technology adoption by individuals and organizations.' The other options — regulation, hardware invention, and manufacturing decline — are not cited as the primary driver in this thesis.

questions.question: The telephone leading to telecom networks is cited as an illustration of which thesis?
options: Technology adoption at scale builds global infrastructures supporting the economy
Discontinuous technology replacement drives industrial disruption
Artificial intelligence is the answer to information overload
New industries emerge from the combination of Big Data and AI
questions.explanation: Thesis #2 holds that as technology gets adopted by larger numbers, global infrastructures get built. The telephone → telecom networks example directly illustrates this. The other options relate to different theses or unrelated concepts.

questions.question: Thesis #3 distinguishes between continuous and discontinuous technology replacement. Which example is explicitly labeled as *discontinuous* in the course material?
options: 5G technology replacing 4G technology
Cloud-based software replacing on-premise IT resources
A smartphone replacing a feature phone
Big data technology replacing traditional storage systems
questions.explanation: The course explicitly labels 'Smart phone replacing feature phone' as discontinuous. The other three examples — 5G/4G, cloud vs. on-premise, big data vs. traditional storage — are listed as part of Thesis #3 but without the 'discontinuous' qualifier, implying they are more incremental/continuous replacements.

questions.question: Thesis #4 states that 'technology itself creates new types of jobs that it shall destroy as it develops further.' Which classical economic theory does this most directly echo?
options: Schumpeter's creative destruction
Keynesian aggregate demand stimulus
Ricardo's comparative advantage in trade
Malthusian resource constraint theory
questions.explanation: Schumpeter's creative destruction describes how innovation continuously creates and destroys economic structures, including jobs and industries. Keynesian theory addresses demand management, Ricardo addresses trade specialization, and Malthus addresses resource limits — none capture the self-destructive innovation cycle described in Thesis #4.

questions.question: The course describes a paradox: abundance of data creates scarcity in another area. What becomes scarce as data volume grows?
options: Storage infrastructure capacity
Open-source software licenses
Human attention and ability to process massive information
Network bandwidth for data transmission
questions.explanation: The course states 'abundance of something (data) creates a scarcity in other areas (attention).' Human cognitive bandwidth — the ability to process information — becomes the scarce resource. Storage, bandwidth, and licenses are supply-side concerns, not the attention scarcity the course highlights.

questions.question: The course frames AI as a potential answer to both rarity (scarce processing capacity) and efficiency challenges. What implicit assumption underlies this framing?
options: AI can perfectly replicate human emotional intelligence
AI's augmented processing capacity can substitute for scarce human cognitive bandwidth
AI will eliminate the production of data at its source
AI renders all human decision-making obsolete
questions.explanation: The course argues that since human processing capacity is scarce and valuable, AI can augment it — providing the rare capability of handling massive information. The other options either overstate AI's role (replacing all decisions) or mischaracterize the problem (eliminating data production or replicating emotions).

questions.question: The IDC Digital Universe report and class discussion suggest that 'more data doesn't necessarily mean more information.' Which explanation best captures this?
options: Data compression algorithms reduce information entropy automatically
Network latency prevents real-time data access and analysis
Without processing capacity and quality filters, data excess creates noise rather than signal
Legal restrictions prevent full utilization of collected data
questions.explanation: The course raises the question of trustworthiness and usefulness of data, and discusses how information overload emerges precisely because volume does not equal value. Compression, latency, and legal issues are distinct technical or regulatory problems not central to this paradox.

questions.question: 'Bad Bots' and 'duplication of data' are cited in class discussion as illustrations of what concern?
options: Technical limitations in parallel computing architectures
Qualitative concerns about how and why data is generated and used
Regulatory gaps in data protection legislation
Inefficiencies in cloud storage pricing models
questions.explanation: These examples appear under 'Quantity & Quality of Data Usages' in the class discussion, illustrating that data is not always trustworthy or purposefully useful. They are not arguments about computing architecture, regulation, or pricing.

questions.question: The Turing Test (1950) was designed to assess:
options: The processing speed of early mainframe computers
Whether a machine can exhibit intelligent behavior indistinguishable from a human
The energy efficiency of AI inference systems
The accuracy of early speech recognition algorithms
questions.explanation: The Turing Test proposes that if a machine's conversational responses are indistinguishable from a human's, the machine can be said to exhibit intelligence. Processing speed, energy efficiency, and speech accuracy are separate engineering concerns.

questions.question: The term 'Artificial Intelligence' was officially coined at which event?
options: The publication of Turing's 1950 paper
Deep Blue's defeat of Kasparov in 1997
The 1956 Dartmouth College conference
The 2018 Turing Prize ceremony for Bengio, Hinton, and LeCun
questions.explanation: The course cites 1956 and the Dartmouth College conference as the moment the term 'Artificial Intelligence' was coined. Turing's 1950 paper introduced the Turing Test but predates the term; Deep Blue and the Turing Prize are much later milestones.

questions.question: According to the White House Report (2016) first classification, a robot that achieves goals via perception, planning, reasoning, and decision-making belongs to which category?
options: Systems that think like humans
Systems that act like humans
Systems that think rationally
Systems that act rationally
questions.explanation: Category (4) — 'Systems that act rationally' — covers intelligent software agents and embodied robots that achieve goals via perception, planning, reasoning, learning, and decision-making. 'Acting like humans' focuses on passing the Turing test; 'thinking' categories focus on cognitive modeling or logic rather than goal-directed action.

questions.question: In the second AI classification ('five tribes'), which tribe uses probabilistic inference?
options: Symbolists
Connectionists
Evolutionaries
Bayesians
questions.explanation: Bayesians use probabilistic inference. Symbolists use logical reasoning based on abstract symbols; Connectionists build brain-inspired structures (neural networks); Evolutionaries use Darwinian methods. Analogizers extrapolate from similar cases.

questions.question: A system using k-nearest neighbor reasoning — matching new inputs to the most similar previously seen cases — belongs to which AI tribe?
options: Symbolist
Connectionist
Evolutionary
Analogizer
questions.explanation: Analogizers 'extrapolate from similar cases seen previously,' which is exactly what k-NN does. Symbolists use explicit rules; Connectionists use neural architectures; Evolutionaries use selection-and-mutation processes.

questions.question: Symbolic AI and Connectionist AI are presented as two fundamental forms of AI. What is the core architectural difference between them?
options: Symbolic AI requires more compute; Connectionist AI requires less data
Symbolic AI uses explicit logical rules and knowledge representations; Connectionist AI learns internal representations from data via neural-like structures
Symbolic AI is restricted to text processing; Connectionist AI handles only image data
Symbolic AI is a recent development; Connectionist AI dates to the 1950s
questions.explanation: The fundamental divide is: Symbolic AI encodes knowledge explicitly as rules/symbols (GOFAI, expert systems); Connectionist AI learns distributed representations from data (neural networks, deep learning). The other options mischaracterize the history, data modality, or compute requirements.

questions.question: The third AI classification (White House Report) includes 'knowledge representation' as a category. Which of the following would NOT belong to this category?
options: Ontologies describing domain concepts and their relationships
Expert system rule bases encoding domain knowledge
Semantic networks linking concepts
Gradient descent optimization of neural network weights
questions.explanation: Gradient descent is an optimization algorithm used in neural network training — it falls under Machine Learning/Deep Learning, not knowledge representation. Ontologies, rule bases, and semantic networks are all knowledge representation formalisms.

questions.question: ANI (Artificial Narrow Intelligence) and AGI (Artificial General Intelligence) are distinguished primarily by:
options: The size of the training dataset used during development
Whether a single technique or a combination of techniques is needed to solve problems beyond a limited scope
The hardware platform on which the system is deployed
Whether supervised or unsupervised learning is the primary training method
questions.explanation: The course explains: 'as soon as there is a need to solve problems beyond the limited scope of a given AI technique, then several AI techniques need to be combined' — this is what motivates AGI. ANI handles a specific task with one technique; AGI requires multi-technique integration for general problem-solving. Dataset size and hardware are not the defining criteria.

questions.question: Arthur Samuel's 1962 checkers-playing program is cited as an early ANI illustration. What specific capability made it significant?
options: It used purely symbolic rule-based logic with hand-crafted heuristics
It incorporated self-learning capabilities
It demonstrated reasoning that generalized across multiple game types
It passed the Turing Test for conversational game commentary
questions.explanation: The course states that Arthur Samuel 'created in 1962 a computer program designed to play checkers, based on self-learning capabilities.' This is notable as an early ML example. It was task-specific (ANI), not general across games, and did not pass the Turing Test.

questions.question: In the Narrow AI subtype classification, 'Limited Memory AI' differs from 'Reactive Machine AI' in which key respect?
options: Limited Memory AI plans for future scenarios without referencing past data
Limited Memory AI uses past experience to inform current decisions
Reactive Machine AI processes sequential data streams over time
Reactive Machine AI relies on Bayesian inference over stored observations
questions.explanation: Reactive Machine AI responds only to current inputs with no memory of past interactions. Limited Memory AI extends this by incorporating past observations to improve current responses (e.g., self-driving cars using recent sensor history). The other options invert or mischaracterize these definitions.

questions.question: AlphaGo's 2016 victory is listed as a milestone. What made Go a significantly harder challenge for AI than chess (Deep Blue, 1997)?
options: Go has fewer pieces, making pattern recognition more difficult
Go's enormous search space makes exhaustive tree search computationally intractable, requiring neural pattern evaluation
Chess was solved by symbolic AI alone, while Go required only reinforcement learning
Go matches are played in real time while chess allows unlimited thinking time
questions.explanation: Go has a branching factor roughly 250 times larger than chess (approximately 250 legal moves per position vs. 35 for chess), making brute-force search impossible. AlphaGo required deep neural networks combined with Monte Carlo tree search. The other options contain factual inaccuracies about piece counts, real-time play, or the role of symbolic AI in chess.

questions.question: Machine Learning is defined in the course as the study of algorithms and statistical models that perform tasks:
options: Using explicit step-by-step programming instructions written by engineers
Without explicit instructions, relying on patterns and inference instead
Only when supervised by human operators in real time
Based exclusively on symbolic logic and hand-crafted rule sets
questions.explanation: The Wikipedia definition cited in the course: 'ML is the scientific study of algorithms and statistical models that computer systems use to perform a specific task without using explicit instructions, relying on patterns and inference instead.' Options A and D describe rule-based programming; option C confuses human oversight with ML's operating principle.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT listed as a learning method in the course's ML taxonomy?
options: Reinforcement learning
Anomaly detection
Supervised learning
Causal inference
questions.explanation: The course lists: supervised learning, unsupervised learning, reinforcement learning, self learning, feature learning, sparse dictionary learning, anomaly detection, and association rules. Causal inference is a separate statistical methodology not included in this taxonomy.

questions.question: Deep Learning is distinguished from broader Machine Learning primarily by its reliance on:
options: Decision trees and ensemble methods such as random forests
Artificial Neural Networks with representation learning
Purely rule-based symbolic expert systems
Bayesian probabilistic graphical models
questions.explanation: The course defines DL as 'part of a broader family of machine learning methods based on artificial neural networks with representation learning.' Decision trees and random forests are classical ML but not DL. Rule-based systems are GOFAI. Bayesian models are a separate ML paradigm.

questions.question: In ML, the distinction between 'training data' and 'test data' serves what fundamental purpose?
options: Training data is used for production deployment; test data for development iterations
Training data teaches the model parameters; test data evaluates generalization to unseen examples
Both are used interchangeably during hyperparameter optimization
Test data is used to correct labeling errors in the training set
questions.explanation: Training data is used to fit model parameters; test data — which the model has never seen — measures how well the learned patterns generalize. Option A inverts the roles. Option C describes cross-validation, not the train/test distinction. Option D conflates data cleaning with evaluation.

questions.question: DL and ML share one critical requirement that differentiates them from most traditional AI techniques. What is it?
options: Real-time data streaming architecture
Deployment exclusively on GPU clusters
Use of large datasets
Integration with blockchain for data provenance
questions.explanation: The course explicitly states: 'DL and ML have in common the use of LARGE DATA SETS.' Traditional AI (GOFAI, expert systems) can function with small, hand-curated knowledge bases. GPU deployment and streaming are implementation choices, not defining requirements.

questions.question: The NLP rules-based pipeline (speech → phonemes → text database → document) has a fundamental limitation compared to LLM-based NLP. What is it?
options: Rules-based NLP cannot handle audio input formats
Rules-based NLP requires hand-crafted linguistic rules and fails to generalize flexibly across diverse language contexts
Rules-based NLP lacks access to any training data
Rules-based NLP can only process a single language
questions.explanation: Rules-based NLP depends on manually engineered phoneme databases, tokenization rules, and text-to-speech mappings. It cannot generalize to new contexts without human-authored updates. LLMs learn flexible representations from data. Options A, C, and D are not correct generalizations — rules-based systems can handle audio input and multiple languages via rule sets.

questions.question: Deep Neural Networks use 'representation learning.' What does this mean in practice?
options: The network memorizes all training examples verbatim as a lookup table
The network learns hierarchical feature representations automatically from raw data, without manual feature engineering
The network applies manually engineered features to structured tabular inputs
The network uses symbolic logic to represent domain knowledge
questions.explanation: Representation learning means the network autonomously discovers useful internal representations (features) at multiple levels of abstraction from raw data — e.g., pixels → edges → shapes → objects in vision. This eliminates the need for manual feature engineering. Options A, C, and D describe memorization, classical ML pipelines, or symbolic AI respectively.

questions.question: The course notes that ML accuracy is 'largely dependent on the size of training data sets.' What does this imply specifically for medical AI applications?
options: Medical AI is the easiest domain to train because patient records are digitized and abundant
Building comprehensive medical training ensembles is 'gruesomely difficult' due to data scarcity and sensitivity constraints
Medical AI can bypass the data size requirement by using rule-based expert systems instead
Reinforcement learning fully circumvents the large-data requirement in clinical settings
questions.explanation: The course states: 'for some specific cases (for instance, in medical applications) building such comprehensive training data ensembles may turn out to be gruesomely difficult.' This reflects that medical data is scarce, privacy-protected, and expensive to label. Options C and D are incorrect — neither expert systems nor RL fundamentally eliminate the data dependency.

questions.question: GOFAI (Good Old-Fashioned AI) is defined by which core characteristic?
options: Use of deep neural networks for perceptual tasks
Rules-based expert systems using explicit symbolic knowledge representations
Probabilistic inference over large statistical corpora
Reinforcement learning with environmental feedback loops
questions.explanation: GOFAI refers to the earlier generation of AI built on explicit rules, logic, and symbolic representations — notably expert systems. Deep learning, probabilistic inference, and reinforcement learning are all post-GOFAI paradigms.

questions.question: The question 'Is coexistence of GOFAI and new AI forms possible?' is made urgent by which LLM failure mode?
options: LLMs are too computationally expensive to scale to general use
LLMs hallucinate — producing plausible but factually incorrect outputs — suggesting pure neural approaches have fundamental, possibly intractable limits
GOFAI systems have been deprecated from all production deployments
New AI forms cannot process structured knowledge bases
questions.explanation: The course cites: 'large language models continue to get things wrong, and the problem is intractable — these phenomena are known as hallucinations.' This motivates neuro-symbolic AI as a hybrid. Options A, C, and D are either inaccurate or irrelevant to the coexistence question.

questions.question: Neuro-symbolic AI is proposed as a response to LLM hallucinations. What does it specifically integrate?
options: Hardware acceleration with software-level optimization layers
Neural learning architectures with symbolic reasoning architectures
Supervised learning pipelines with unsupervised clustering modules
Cloud infrastructure management with on-premise expert system deployment
questions.explanation: Wikipedia (cited in the course): 'Neuro-symbolic AI integrates neural and symbolic AI architectures to address the weaknesses of each, providing a robust AI capable of reasoning, learning, and cognitive modeling.' The other options combine unrelated technical layers.

questions.question: Y. LeCun's 2023 position concerns 'sensory grounding for meaning and understanding' in LLMs. What fundamental critique does this represent?
options: LLMs consume too much energy during inference operations
LLMs lack grounding in physical and sensory experience, which may limit genuine semantic understanding
LLMs cannot process multimodal inputs such as images and audio
LLMs require more parameters to achieve human-level commonsense reasoning
questions.explanation: LeCun's 'grounding' argument is that language-only models lack contact with the physical world — they manipulate statistical word patterns without embodied understanding. Options A and D concern scale/efficiency; option C is factually false (multimodal LLMs exist and predate the critique).

questions.question: The philosophical side of the class discussion references 'ontology.' In AI, an ontology refers to:
options: The chronological history and milestones of AI research
A formal representation of knowledge as a set of concepts, categories, and their relationships
The ethical framework governing responsible AI deployment
The process of training neural networks on symbolically annotated datasets
questions.explanation: In AI and knowledge engineering, an ontology is a formal specification of concepts and relationships in a domain — used in symbolic AI for knowledge representation. It is not a history, an ethics framework, or a training method.

questions.question: The original three Vs of Big Data, as defined in the course, are:
options: Value, Velocity, Virtualization
Volume, Variety, Velocity
Veracity, Visualization, Volume
Variety, Validity, Velocity
questions.explanation: The course explicitly states: 'Big data was originally associated with three key concepts: volume, variety, and velocity.' The other combinations include V-words that were added later (veracity, value) or are not part of the canonical Big Data vocabulary (visualization, virtualization, validity).

questions.question: Hadoop is a core Big Data technology. What fundamentally distinguishes it from traditional relational database management systems?
options: Hadoop requires strict schema-on-write before any data can be ingested
Hadoop is designed for distributed processing of very large, potentially unstructured datasets across commodity hardware
Hadoop is exclusively optimized for real-time streaming data processing
Hadoop replaces in-memory processing with disk-only sequential operations for reliability
questions.explanation: Hadoop's HDFS and MapReduce framework distributes both storage and computation across many nodes, enabling processing of datasets too large for single machines. Traditional RDBMS rely on schema-on-write and vertical scaling. Hadoop is not limited to streaming, and it does not eliminate in-memory processing (Spark adds that capability on top).

questions.question: NoSQL databases differ from traditional SQL databases primarily in that they:
options: Cannot handle structured data under any circumstances
Sacrifice strict ACID guarantees for horizontal scalability and schema flexibility
Are designed exclusively for graph-structured data
Require NewSQL middleware to achieve distributed operation
questions.explanation: NoSQL databases prioritize availability and scalability (CAP theorem trade-offs) over strict consistency, and they accommodate flexible schemas (document, key-value, column-family, graph). They can handle structured data (option A is false). Not all NoSQL databases are graph databases (option C). NewSQL is a different category that adds distributed SQL capabilities (option D).

questions.question: The course lists 'LLM, RAG, AI Agents' alongside Hadoop and NoSQL in the Big Data/AI technologies section. What does this co-listing imply about the current landscape?
options: LLMs are simply a rebranding of NoSQL document stores
Modern AI infrastructure is converging with and layering on top of Big Data engineering stacks
RAG technology completely replaces the need for traditional data pipelines
Streaming technology is deprecated in favor of LLM-based batch processing
questions.explanation: Placing LLMs and RAG alongside Hadoop, NoSQL, and streaming indicates that modern AI systems build on and integrate with existing Big Data infrastructure. LLMs are architecturally different from NoSQL stores. RAG extends rather than replaces pipelines. Streaming technology remains active and relevant.

questions.question: 'In-Memory processing' is listed as a key Big Data technology. What specific bottleneck does it address compared to disk-based processing?
options: Network latency between distributed cluster nodes
I/O latency — RAM access is orders of magnitude faster than disk, enabling real-time analytics
CPU instruction cycle limitations in parallel computing
Bandwidth constraints in machine-to-machine sensor communication
questions.explanation: In-memory processing (e.g., Apache Spark vs. MapReduce) moves working data into RAM instead of reading from and writing to disk between each computation step. Disk I/O is the primary bottleneck it eliminates. Network latency, CPU limitations, and M2M bandwidth are separate bottlenecks addressed by other architectural choices.

questions.question: The MAD 2025 landscape is described as featuring 'a large variety of frameworks, architectures, technologies.' What is the primary strategic challenge this creates for adopting organizations?
options: It forces all companies to build proprietary tools internally
It creates vendor lock-in through open standards
It makes selecting, integrating, and maintaining the right technology stack extremely complex
It leads to full standardization that eliminates competitive differentiation
questions.explanation: The 'complex world' framing highlights that the sheer variety of options — storage, databases, analytics, AI, open vs. proprietary — creates decision complexity and integration challenges. Building everything in-house, vendor lock-in through open standards, and full standardization are all contradicted by the landscape's fragmentation.

questions.question: Generative AI models produce outputs based on:
options: Manually crafted rule sets encoding domain-specific knowledge
Learning underlying patterns and structures from training data and generating new data from prompts
Direct retrieval from pre-indexed databases without any generation step
Human-in-the-loop annotation performed at inference time
questions.explanation: Wikipedia's definition (cited in the course): Generative AI 'uses generative models to produce text, images, videos, or other forms of data. These models learn the underlying patterns and structures of their training data and use them to produce new data based on the input, which often comes in the form of natural language prompts.' Rules-based systems, pure retrieval (like search), and human annotation are all non-generative.

questions.question: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) addresses which core limitation of standard LLMs?
options: LLMs cannot process natural language queries without structured prompts
LLMs cannot generate text beyond a fixed context window length
LLMs lack access to domain-specific or recently updated information not present in their training data
LLMs are architecturally incompatible with cloud-based deployment infrastructure
questions.explanation: RAG's Wikipedia definition (cited in the course): it 'enables LLMs to retrieve and incorporate new information from external data sources... allowing LLMs to use domain-specific and/or updated information that is not available in the training data.' Options A and B mischaracterize how LLMs work; option D is factually false.

questions.question: The transformer architecture is described as the foundation of GenAI. What most distinguishes it from earlier sequence models such as RNNs?
options: Transformers process tokens sequentially while maintaining recurrent hidden states
Transformers use attention mechanisms enabling parallel processing of entire input sequences
Transformers require significantly smaller datasets than RNNs for comparable performance
Transformers were originally designed exclusively for image generation tasks
questions.explanation: The transformer's self-attention mechanism allows it to process all tokens in a sequence simultaneously and model long-range dependencies directly, unlike RNNs which process tokens sequentially and struggle with long-range dependencies. Transformers actually require more data than RNNs, and they were originally designed for NLP (not images).

questions.question: RAG systems 'first refer to a specified set of documents, then respond to user queries.' What core priority does this architectural choice reflect?
options: Faster inference speed by caching common query responses
Reduced hallucination risk by grounding responses in retrieved, verifiable source documents
Lower hardware requirements by offloading computation to external document stores
Broader coverage of unseen language patterns not in the parametric model
questions.explanation: RAG's purpose is to anchor model responses in specific, retrievable documents — reducing the reliance on potentially stale or incorrect parametric knowledge that causes hallucinations. It does not primarily target inference speed, hardware reduction, or language coverage.

questions.question: The course notes that 'biased or inaccurate training data can make an LLM's output less reliable.' How does RAG partially mitigate this issue?
options: RAG retrains the base LLM dynamically on curated corpora after each query
RAG allows the model to reference authoritative external documents at inference time, partially bypassing stale or biased parametric knowledge
RAG eliminates the need for pre-training the underlying language model entirely
RAG uses reinforcement learning to detect and correct biased outputs before they are shown to users
questions.explanation: RAG retrieves up-to-date, authoritative source documents at query time and conditions the LLM's response on them. This means the model can override or supplement its potentially biased parametric knowledge with verified external content. RAG does not retrain the model, eliminate pre-training, or use RL for bias correction.

questions.question: ChatGPT reached 100 million users in 2 months versus Netflix's approximately 120 months. In the context of digital transformation theory, what does this adoption rate primarily illustrate?
options: The inherent superiority of conversational AI over streaming entertainment services
The accelerating pace of technology adoption as mature global digital infrastructure lowers barriers to entry
The commercial failure of subscription-based media business models
That consumer AI is structurally more viral than subscription services regardless of context
questions.explanation: The example illustrates Thesis #2's implication: as global digital infrastructure (internet, smartphones, payment systems) matures, new technologies can reach mass adoption far faster. This is not a claim about AI superiority over entertainment, media business model failure, or an unconditional virality law.

questions.question: Among the GenAI companies listed, Anthropic (Claude), OpenAI (ChatGPT), Meta (Llama), and DeepSeek represent different geopolitical origins. What strategic implication does this diversity raise?
options: AI development is now fully commoditized with no remaining competitive differentiation
National AI strategies and geopolitical competition are actively shaping the global foundation model landscape
All major LLMs converge on identical architectures, making origin irrelevant to performance
Open-source models like Llama will imminently and completely displace closed proprietary models
questions.explanation: The course's vertical integration section (GAFAM/BATX, Anthropic/OpenAI/DeepSeek) signals that AI is a strategic national and corporate priority with geopolitical dimensions. AI is not commoditized; architectures differ; and the open vs. closed model debate remains unresolved.

questions.question: In the traditional Big Data value chain, 'data integration' refers to:
options: Selling processed data assets to third-party data brokers
Establishing a common view of disparate data from multiple heterogeneous sources
Real-time streaming of IoT sensor data into central repositories
Training ML models on labeled datasets extracted from operational databases
questions.explanation: The course defines data integration as 'the ability to establish a common view of disparate data.' This is the ETL/data warehousing layer of the value chain. Data brokerage, streaming, and ML training are separate value chain activities.

questions.question: In the emerging GenAI value chain, 'Foundation Model Providers' occupy which layer?
options: Hardware infrastructure (chips, GPUs)
Cloud hyperscaler services (AWS, Azure, GCP)
The creators of base pre-trained large models (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta)
Application-layer vertical SaaS solutions (Harvey, Jasper)
questions.explanation: The course places Foundation Model Providers as layer 3, described as 'The Creators': OpenAI, Anthropic, Google (Gemini), Meta (Llama), Mistral. Hardware is layer 1; cloud hyperscalers are layer 2; vertical SaaS companies are layer 5.

questions.question: The 'Token Economy' in GenAI business models represents a shift away from which previous SaaS pricing paradigm?
options: Revenue-sharing arrangements with training data providers
Per-user subscription pricing, toward pricing per unit of processed text or data
One-time perpetual software license fees
Hardware-bundled software pricing models
questions.explanation: The course states: 'Pricing is moving away from per user toward per token (units of text/data).' Traditional SaaS was per-user subscriptions. Revenue sharing with data owners is a separate emerging dynamic. Perpetual licenses and hardware bundles predate SaaS entirely.

questions.question: The 'Hardware Bottleneck' described in the GenAI business model means GPU supply constraints set costs. What economic phenomenon does this reflect?
options: Perfect competition in the semiconductor market driving prices to marginal cost
A supply-constrained market where physical resource scarcity grants pricing power to hardware providers
Demand destruction from cloud overcapacity reducing infrastructure spending
Natural monopoly formation in cloud hyperscaler services
questions.explanation: The course states: 'because GPU supply is limited, the cost is often dictated by hardware availability rather than software competition.' This is a classic supply-constrained market where scarcity, not marginal cost competition, sets prices — giving NVIDIA in particular exceptional pricing power. There is no perfect competition or demand destruction in this context.

questions.question: Data owners like Reddit and Getty Images are increasingly demanding licensing fees from foundation model providers. Which implicit assumption of early AI value chain models does this challenge?
options: That training data would always be user-generated and freely available for commercial use
That inference costs would continuously decrease over successive model generations
That cloud providers would indefinitely subsidize the cost of model training
That open-source models would dominate over proprietary commercial models
questions.explanation: The course notes: 'Data Owners are increasingly becoming entities in the business model, demanding licensing fees.' Early AI value chain models implicitly assumed that internet-scraped, user-generated content was freely available for training. This assumption is now being contested legally and commercially.

questions.question: The tension between 'specialization vs. vertical integration' in the AI business model mirrors which classic industrial economics dilemma?
options: Whether to patent AI algorithms or release them open-source
Whether to control the full stack for competitive advantage versus focusing on a single layer of the value chain
Whether to adopt per-token or per-user pricing for AI services
Whether national or global regulatory standards should govern AI development
questions.explanation: Vertical integration — from chips (NVIDIA) through cloud (AWS) to models (OpenAI) to applications — versus horizontal specialization at one layer is a classic 'make vs. buy' and 'integrated vs. modular' industrial economics question. Patent strategy, pricing, and regulation are separate strategic dimensions.

questions.question: The 2018 McKinsey data showed marketing-focused AI adoption. By 2024–2025 (BOND report), AI usage has become cross-company. What does this evolution primarily indicate?
options: Marketing AI tools have become technologically obsolete
AI has transitioned from a functional-specific efficiency tool to a general-purpose enterprise technology
Companies have consolidated all AI investment into R&D departments
AI adoption has plateaued following initial marketing use case saturation
questions.explanation: The shift from marketing-only AI to cross-functional enterprise AI is consistent with AI maturing into a General Purpose Technology (GPT) — the first triple-challenge theme. GPTs move from specific applications to pervasive use across the economy. Marketing tools are not obsolete; investment is broadening, not consolidating.

questions.question: 'Explainability' as a barrier to ML adoption refers to the fact that ML systems:
options: Are too slow for real-time decision support applications
Often appear as a 'black box' — their internal reasoning is opaque to non-specialist users
Require excessive labeled data before producing any meaningful output
Cannot process unstructured data formats such as text and images
questions.explanation: The course defines explainability as the issue that 'AI and ML techniques appear, very often, to non-specialist users to be a black-box type of a business-support system.' Speed, data requirements, and data format handling are separate technical concerns.

questions.question: Data labeling in supervised learning is described as 'extremely time-consuming' and error-prone. What direct risk does this create for ML models?
options: Overfitting caused by excessive compute resources devoted to label verification
Poor label quality directly degrades model accuracy — garbage in, garbage out
Underfitting caused by insufficient model architectural complexity
Hardware failures triggered by processing large annotation file formats
questions.explanation: The course notes that labeling 'may generate errors' and requires 'massive investments in human labor.' In supervised learning, the model learns from labels — if labels are wrong or inconsistent, the model learns incorrect mappings. This is the classic GIGO (garbage in, garbage out) principle. Overfitting and underfitting have separate causes.

questions.question: Bias in the context of AI is defined in the course as:
options: Systematic deviation in hardware processing performance under load
The likelihood of systematically producing erroneous results or reaching wrong conclusions
Random statistical noise present in any finite training dataset
Overfitting to minority class examples in imbalanced classification datasets
questions.explanation: The course definition: 'Bias, in the context of AI, is related to the likelihood of, systematically, producing erroneous results, or reaching wrong conclusions.' The key qualifier is 'systematically' — bias is a repeatable, directional error, not random noise (option C) or an overfitting artifact (option D).

questions.question: Bias can be 'rooted both in data and in the computer model.' Which of the following best exemplifies model-level bias distinct from data-level bias?
options: A training dataset collected exclusively from a non-representative demographic group
An algorithm that systematically favors one outcome due to its objective function or inductive bias, independent of the input data distribution
Missing outcome labels in a training dataset causing systematic gaps
Duplicate records in training data inflating the frequency of certain patterns
questions.explanation: Data-level bias comes from the training data itself (options A, C, D). Model-level bias refers to the algorithm's structural assumptions — its inductive biases, regularization choices, or objective function — that can systematically skew predictions regardless of how representative the data is.

questions.question: El-Mhamdi et al. (2023) argue that 'high accuracy requires memorizing large training datasets,' and that this creates a safety vulnerability. Why?
options: Memorization prevents any generalization to new, unseen inputs
Memorized content from heterogeneous, user-generated data exposes models to data poisoning — LLMs 'repeat and amplify' training data including malicious injections
Large memorized datasets significantly slow inference time to unacceptable levels
Memorization violates copyright law in all major jurisdictions
questions.explanation: The course cites: 'LLMs are stochastic parrots that repeat and amplify their training data, strongly encouraging data poisoning, and may be manipulated by this poisoning.' The safety risk is that memorization of heterogeneous, user-generated data — including data from malicious actors — makes LLMs vulnerable to adversarial manipulation. Options A, C, and D are either inaccurate or distinct concerns.

questions.question: Shumailov et al. (Nature, 2024) found that 'AI models collapse when trained on recursively generated data.' What does model collapse imply for the long-term AI ecosystem?
options: Recursive training progressively improves model efficiency and specialization
Training on AI-generated outputs leads to progressive degradation of model quality, diversity, and accuracy over successive generations
Models trained on synthetic data become more robust to adversarial inputs
Model collapse is a purely theoretical concern with no empirical confirmation
questions.explanation: The Nature paper (cited in the course) empirically demonstrates that models trained on recursively generated (AI-produced) data progressively forget the true data distribution and converge on lower-quality, less diverse outputs — a compounding degradation. Option A inverts the finding; option C is contradicted by the evidence; option D is false (it was published in Nature with empirical results).

questions.question: The explainability barrier is described as particularly impactful 'when the expected output informs decision-making.' In which scenario would it be MOST critical?
options: A recommendation engine suggesting movies based on viewing history
An AI system informing medical diagnostics or judicial sentencing decisions
A generative AI tool drafting marketing copy from product descriptions
An anomaly detection system flagging unusual patterns in network traffic logs
questions.explanation: When AI informs high-stakes, irreversible decisions — medical diagnoses, criminal sentencing — opacity is critically dangerous because errors can harm individuals and stakeholders need to understand and contest the reasoning. Movie recommendations and marketing copy are low-stakes; network anomaly detection, while important, does not carry the same irreversible personal harm.

questions.question: The course cites the Institut Montaigne report on algorithmic bias and describes it as 'the most impeding hurdle.' Why is algorithmic bias ranked above explainability and data labeling as an adoption barrier?
options: Bias is more financially expensive to remediate than infrastructure or compute barriers
Bias generates repeatable, systematic errors that can produce discriminatory, unfair, or illegal outcomes — simultaneously creating regulatory, ethical, and reputational risks
Bias affects only supervised learning, which limits its overall scope relative to other ML paradigms
Bias is uniquely difficult to measure quantitatively compared to explainability or labeling challenges
questions.explanation: The course states bias 'generates repeatable errors that may lead to erroneous, unfair, discriminatory, potentially dangerous, or illegal conclusions and/or actions.' This multi-dimensional risk — legal, ethical, social, reputational — compounds across all stakeholders. Options A and D may be partially true but are not the course's stated rationale. Option C is false — bias affects all ML paradigms.

questions.question: AI as a 'General Purpose Technology' is compared to electricity and the internet. This framing implies that AI's economic impact will be:
options: Confined to narrow vertical applications in technology-intensive sectors
Broad, transformative, and disruptive across multiple industries and institutions simultaneously
Primarily limited to efficiency gains in manufacturing supply chains
Strong in the short term but self-limiting as the technology matures
questions.explanation: GPTs — electricity, steam, IT, and now AI — are characterized by pervasive applicability across sectors, spawning complementary innovations and restructuring entire economies. The course explicitly cites: 'existing economic institutions shall be substantially altered.' Options A, C, and D all understate the expected reach of a GPT.
questions.category: Triple Challenge & Dark Side of AI

questions.question: The concept of 'division of learning' (Zuboff) in the AI context refers to:
options: The technical gap between deep learning and classical machine learning capabilities
The knowledge gap between those who understand data-driven systems and those who merely produce data without understanding it
The division of training data between supervised and unsupervised learning subsets
The institutional separation between AI research in academia and commercial deployment
questions.explanation: The course cites Shoshana Zuboff's concept: 'Is there a barrier between the ability to access, understand, and benefit from this data, and the practice of simply producing it?' The division of learning describes asymmetric knowledge power — some actors understand and benefit from AI systems while others simply generate the data they run on.
questions.category: Triple Challenge & Dark Side of AI

questions.question: The question of whether an AI chatbot should be 'considered an economic agent in its own right' relates to which concept in public policy theory?
options: Market failure and the need for Pigouvian externality corrections
Intermediation and agency — whether AI acts as a neutral conduit or an active agent shaping social relationships
Antitrust regulation of technology platform monopolies
Intellectual property rights over AI-generated content authorship
questions.explanation: The course defines public action instruments as devices that 'organize specific social relationships between public authorities and their recipients.' The agency question is: does an AI chatbot merely relay information (neutral conduit) or actively shape the interaction (economic/social agent)? Externalities, antitrust, and IP are distinct policy concerns.
questions.category: Triple Challenge & Dark Side of AI

questions.question: The 'dark side' of AI includes the combination of deepfakes and algorithmic micro-targeting. How do these two technologies create a compound threat beyond either alone?
options: Deepfakes reduce social media engagement while micro-targeting amplifies it, creating measurement confusion
Deepfakes generate fabricated audiovisual content while micro-targeting ensures it reaches the most susceptible audiences with maximum persuasive precision
Both are primarily defensive cybersecurity technologies repurposed for offense
Micro-targeting neutralizes deepfakes by filtering synthetic media from targeted feeds
questions.explanation: The course states that deepfakes 'may become effective tools for disseminating fabricated political messages in the wrong hands, made even more persuasive with algorithmic micro-targeting.' Deepfakes are the weapon; micro-targeting is the precision delivery mechanism. Together they create scalable, personalized disinformation that is far more dangerous than either alone.
questions.category: Triple Challenge & Dark Side of AI

questions.question: The course quotes Brynjolfsson & McAfee (2017): ML is 'the most important general-purpose technology of our era.' What critical condition must hold for this claim to fully materialize?
options: All competing technologies must become obsolete to clear adoption barriers
Complementary investments in human capital, organizational redesign, and institutional adaptation must accompany ML deployment
ML must achieve Artificial General Intelligence within a decade
Hardware costs must approach zero through Moore's Law continuation
questions.explanation: Economic research on GPTs (Brynjolfsson, David) consistently shows that GPT productivity gains materialize only when organizations co-invest in complementary changes: retraining workers, redesigning processes, and updating institutions. The technology alone is insufficient. AGI, obsolescence of other technologies, and zero hardware costs are not conditions identified in the course material.
questions.category: Triple Challenge & Dark Side of AI

questions.question: 'AI as Digital Transformation driver' raises the question of where the frontier lies between activities that should remain human and those that can be delegated to machines. This question is fundamentally about:
options: Optimizing labor costs through automation of repetitive tasks
The ethical and social boundaries of human agency versus algorithmic delegation in consequential decisions
Identifying which job categories will experience the highest wage growth from AI
Determining the technical performance threshold at which AI surpasses human accuracy
questions.explanation: The course frames this as a 'fundamental question' related to the 'division of learning' and human agency, not merely a cost optimization or performance benchmarking exercise. It concerns which decisions, knowledge, and responsibilities should remain with humans versus being delegated to machines — a question that is inherently normative and social.
questions.category: Triple Challenge & Dark Side of AI

questions.question: Which role in a data-driven organization is primarily responsible for ensuring compliance with data protection regulations?
options: Chief Data Officer (CDO)
Data Scientist
Data Protection Officer (DPO)
BI Manager
questions.explanation: The Data Protection Officer (DPO) is specifically responsible for data protection compliance — under frameworks like GDPR in Europe. The CDO focuses on data strategy and value extraction; the Data Scientist focuses on analytical modeling; the BI Manager focuses on business intelligence reporting.

questions.question: The WEF Future of Jobs reports (2020 and 2025) are cited in the context of AI's labor market impact. What overarching trend do they illustrate?
options: AI will exclusively create new jobs in the technology sector
AI simultaneously eliminates certain roles, transforms others, and creates new ones across the labor market
Job displacement from AI remains a theoretical risk with no empirical labor market evidence yet
Only low-skill, routine jobs face meaningful risk of automation
questions.explanation: The WEF reports, consistent with Thesis #4, show a complex, multi-directional effect: some jobs disappear, others are transformed, and new categories emerge. The impact is not confined to low-skill work — many cognitive and professional tasks are also affected.

questions.question: The Data Steward role in data-driven organizations is distinct from a Data Scientist in what primary respect?
options: Data Stewards build predictive models; Data Scientists manage regulatory compliance
Data Stewards focus on data quality, governance, and lifecycle management; Data Scientists focus on extracting analytical and predictive insights
Data Stewards manage cloud database infrastructure; Data Scientists handle on-premise systems
Data Stewards work exclusively with structured relational data; Data Scientists handle only unstructured data
questions.explanation: Data Stewards own data quality, metadata, and governance policies across the data lifecycle. Data Scientists use data to build models and derive insights. The distinction is governance/quality (stewardship) versus analytics/modeling (science). Options C and D mischaracterize scope; option A inverts the roles.

questions.question: The value chain distinguishes between 'Users,' 'Operators/Managers,' and 'Creators' of data. A media company producing original content that is then scraped to train foundation models occupies which dual role?
options: Simultaneous User and Operator of data
Creator and, increasingly, a contested data asset whose content is incorporated into Foundation Model training without clear compensation
Operator and Manager only — media companies do not create data directly
Creator and exclusive Regulator of their produced content
questions.explanation: Media companies are Creators of original content (journalism, entertainment). As AI companies scrape this content to train LLMs, media companies find themselves involuntary data assets in the emerging GenAI value chain — leading to the licensing disputes cited in the course. They are not Users/Operators in the traditional sense, and they have no regulatory authority.

questions.question: In the combinatorial effects framework (IoT, Blockchain, Big Data, AI), which of the extended Vs does Blockchain specifically address?
options: Volume — by providing distributed storage capacity
Variety — by standardizing heterogeneous data formats
Velocity — by accelerating transaction confirmation times
inViolability — by providing data integrity, immutability, and tamper-resistance
questions.explanation: The course lists five Vs in the combinatorial framework: Volume (IoT), Variety (Big Data), Velocity (Big Data/AI), inViolability (Blockchain), and Veracity/Value (AI). Blockchain's core contribution is immutable, cryptographically secured records — data inViolability and trustworthiness in a decentralized environment.

questions.question: In the IoT-Blockchain-BigData-AI convergent stack, what does Blockchain contribute that neither Big Data nor AI can provide on its own?
options: Real-time data ingestion from heterogeneous connected objects
Neural pattern recognition across large unstructured datasets
Decentralized trust and immutable transaction records across distributed participants without a central authority
Natural language interfaces for querying sensor data streams
questions.explanation: Blockchain's unique contribution is trustless, decentralized consensus and immutable ledgers — enabling verification and trust in distributed networks without relying on a central trusted intermediary. Big Data handles volume/velocity; AI handles pattern recognition/intelligence; IoT handles data generation. None of the others provide decentralized trust.

questions.question: The adoption discussion uses QWERTY and MS-DOS as examples of 'installed base' effects. What technology adoption concept do these illustrate?
options: Network effects driving winner-take-all market concentration
Path dependency — early adoption of a standard creates lock-in that resists superior alternatives even when they emerge
Dominant design emerging through competitive market selection of the optimal design
S-curve diffusion where adoption accelerates after a critical mass is reached
questions.explanation: QWERTY persists despite arguably better keyboard layouts; MS-DOS dominated despite technical limitations. These are classic examples of path dependency — where historical adoption decisions create switching costs and network effects that lock in suboptimal standards. Network effects (option A), dominant design (option C), and S-curves (option D) are related but distinct concepts.

questions.question: The course notes that DC and AC electricity and symbolic/connectionist AI were 'initially considered rival technologies' that ultimately coexisted. What broader lesson does this hold for the current LLM vs. symbolic AI debate?
options: One paradigm always ultimately defeats the other through superior performance metrics
Apparently competing technological paradigms may discover complementary roles within a larger ecosystem — as reflected in the emergence of neuro-symbolic AI
Market consolidation will inevitably produce a single dominant winner in AI architectures
Coexistence is only possible when technologies operate in entirely separate, non-overlapping application domains
questions.explanation: The course explicitly uses DC/AC and symbolic/connectionist coexistence as adoption lessons. The modern equivalent — neuro-symbolic AI — embodies exactly this principle: combining neural learning and symbolic reasoning rather than one defeating the other. Markets have not forced a single winner in electricity or early AI paradigms, and application domain separation is not the condition for coexistence.
